title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: "Well, then, what's the plan of campaign? Tell us everything," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.

"Here's the plan. Right now we're driving to Gvozdyov. At Gvozdyov, on this side, there's a grouse marsh, and on the other side of the village there are some magnificent snipe marshes, where there are also grouse. It's hot now, and we'll get there toward evening — it's about fifteen miles — and do some evening shooting; we'll spend the night there and go on tomorrow to the bigger moors."
"And there's nothing on the way?"
"Yes, but we ought to save ourselves; besides, it's hot. There are two nice little spots, but I doubt there'll be anything to shoot."

Levin would have liked to stop at those little spots himself, but they were close to home; he could shoot them any time, and they were only little places — there would barely be room for three guns. So, with a bit of dishonesty, he said he doubted there would be anything to shoot. When they reached a small marsh, Levin would have driven straight past, but Stepan Arkadyevitch, with the practiced eye of a sportsman, immediately spotted the reeds from the road.
"Shall we give it a try?" he said, pointing at the little marsh.
"Levin, please! How splendid!" Vassenka Veslovsky began begging, and Levin could only give in.
Before they even had time to stop, the dogs had flown one after the other into the marsh.
"Krak! Laska!..."
The dogs came back.

"There won't be room for three of us. I'll stay here," Levin said, hoping they would find nothing but the peewits that the dogs had startled and that were now turning in flight, wailing plaintively over the marsh.
"No! Come on, Levin, let's go together!" Veslovsky called.
"Really, there's no room. Laska, back, Laska! You don't need another dog, do you?"

Levin stayed behind with the wagonette and watched the sportsmen enviously. They walked clear across the marsh. Apart from little birds and peewits, of which Vassenka shot one, there was nothing in the marsh.
"You see now I wasn't being stingy about the marsh," Levin said, "it was just a waste of time."

"Oh no, it was great fun all the same. Did you see me?" said Vassenka Veslovsky, clambering awkwardly into the wagonette with his gun and his peewit in his hands. "How splendidly I shot that bird! Didn't I? Well, will we soon be at the real spot?"

The horses suddenly jolted forward, Levin knocked his head against the stock of someone's gun, and there was the crack of a shot. Actually the gun went off first, but to Levin it seemed the other way around. It turned out that Vassenka Veslovsky had only pulled one trigger and left the other hammer cocked. The charge flew into the ground without doing any harm. Stepan Arkadyevitch shook his head and laughed reprovingly at Veslovsky, but Levin couldn't bring himself to scold him. For one thing, any rebuke would have looked like a reaction to the danger and the bump now rising on Levin's forehead. And besides, Veslovsky was at first so naively distressed, and then laughed so good-humoredly and infectiously at the general consternation, that you couldn't help laughing with him.

When they reached the second marsh, which was fairly large and would take some time to shoot through, Levin tried to talk them out of stopping. But once again Veslovsky talked him into it. And again, since the marsh was narrow, Levin played the good host and stayed with the carriage.

Krak headed straight for some clumps of sedge. Vassenka Veslovsky was the first to run after the dog. Before Stepan Arkadyevitch had time to catch up, a grouse flew out. Veslovsky missed it, and it flew off into an unmown meadow. That grouse was now left for Veslovsky to follow up. Krak found it again and pointed, Veslovsky shot it, and then went back to the carriage. "Now you go and I'll stay with the horses," he said.
Levin had begun to feel the pangs of a sportsman's envy. He handed the reins to Veslovsky and walked into the marsh.
Laska, who had been whining piteously at the injustice of her treatment, shot straight ahead toward a promising spot Levin knew well, and that Krak had not yet covered.
"Why don't you call her back?" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted.
"She won't scare them," Levin answered, sharing his bitch's excitement and hurrying after her.

The closer Laska got to the familiar nesting places, the more focused her searching became. A little marsh bird distracted her for no more than an instant. She made one circuit of the clump of reeds, was starting a second, and suddenly quivered with excitement and froze.

"Come on, come on, Stiva!" Levin shouted, feeling his heart starting to pound; and suddenly, as though some shutter had been thrown open inside his straining ears, every sound — confused but loud — began to beat against his hearing, all sense of distance lost. He heard Stepan Arkadyevitch's footsteps and mistook them for the distant trampling of the horses; he heard the brittle snap of twigs underfoot and took it for a grouse taking off. He also heard, not far behind him, a splashing in the water that he could not explain to himself.
Picking his way carefully, he moved up to the dog.
"Fetch it!"

Not a grouse but a snipe flew up from beside the dog. Levin had raised his gun, but at the very moment he was taking aim the splashing grew louder, came closer, and merged with the sound of Veslovsky's voice shouting something with strange loudness. Levin saw that he was pointing his gun behind the snipe, but he fired anyway.
Once he was sure he had missed, Levin looked around and saw the horses and the wagonette not on the road but out in the marsh.
Veslovsky, eager to see the shooting, had driven the horses into the marsh, and they had gotten stuck in the mud.

"Damn the fellow!" Levin muttered to himself as he walked back to the carriage sunk in the mire. "What did you drive in there for?" he said dryly to him, and called the coachman over and started hauling the horses out.

Levin was annoyed at having had his shooting interrupted, annoyed at the horses being stuck in the mud, and even more annoyed at the fact that neither Stepan Arkadyevitch nor Veslovsky was helping him and the coachman to unharness the horses and get them out, since neither of them had the faintest idea about harnessing. Without bothering to answer a syllable of Vassenka's protest that the ground had been perfectly dry there, Levin worked in silence with the coachman to get the horses free. But then, as he warmed up to the work and saw how energetically Veslovsky was tugging at the wagonette by one of the mudguards — so hard that he actually broke it — Levin reproached himself for having let yesterday's feelings make him too cold toward Veslovsky, and he tried to be especially friendly to smooth over his earlier chill. Once everything was put right and the carriage was back on the road, Levin had the lunch served.

"_Bon appétit — bonne conscience! Ce poulet va tomber jusqu'au fond de mes bottes_," quoted Vassenka, his spirits restored, as he finished his second chicken. "Well, now our troubles are over, and everything will go beautifully. Only, to atone for my sins, I'm bound to ride on the box. Right? Eh? No, no! I'll be your Automedon. You'll see how I drive you," he replied, not letting go of the rein when Levin asked him to let the coachman drive. "No, I have to atone for my sins, and I'm very comfortable on the box." And so he drove.

Levin was a little worried that he would wear the horses out, especially the chestnut, which Veslovsky did not know how to hold in; but, without realizing it, he came under the spell of his cheerfulness and listened all the way to the songs Veslovsky sang on the box, and to his descriptions and imitations of driving English-style, four-in-hand. So it was in the very best of spirits that they drove on after lunch to the Gvozdyov marsh.
